intro:
The database category on OpenSourceStack is the deepest we curate. Postgres sits at the center of almost every modern stack, which is why we list the engines that build on top of it (Supabase, Directus, Baserow, PocketBase, Parse), the engines that compete with it (MySQL forks, MongoDB, Neo4j, SurrealDB, CockroachDB), and the tools that turn any database into an application backend.

The split we see most often is "do I want a complete backend-in-a-box (Supabase, Appwrite, Parse)" versus "do I want a layer over a database I already operate (Directus, Baserow, NocoDB)". The first group owns your schema and migration story. The second group lets you keep your existing database and adds an API and admin UI on top.

What separates the projects we list from the ones we don't: we only include databases that are actively maintained, have production deployments at scale, and don't lock you into a specific cloud. We've excluded projects that are effectively abandoned (no commits in 12+ months), hobbyist-only (single developer, no users outside the maintainer), or commercial-only with no usable open source edition.
selectionNotes: We test each database in a clean Docker environment with the recommended setup. If it doesn't install in under 30 minutes, it doesn't ship. We then run real queries, real migrations, and check that backups work. The Security Score reflects how the project handles auth, encryption-at-rest, and the project's CVE history.

intro:
Privacy-respecting analytics is one of the most-requested categories on this site. Most teams want to leave Google Analytics but keep the metrics that matter: pageviews, bounce rate, referrers, UTM tracking, custom events. The open source alternatives fall into two camps: lightweight personal/small-team tools (Plausible, Umami, Ackee, Fathom Lite, OWA, GoAccess) and full product-analytics platforms (PostHog, Matomo).

For most websites, the lightweight category is the right starting point. They use 1-3% of the resources of Google Analytics, don't set cookies, are GDPR/CCPA compliant out of the box, and give you real-time dashboards in minutes. Plausible and Umami are the two we recommend first — both have commercial offerings if you don't want to self-host, both are well-maintained, both have first-class WordPress and static-site integrations.

PostHog is the only project we list that's a true Mixpanel/Heap replacement. It bundles product analytics, feature flags, A/B testing, session replay, and surveys in one platform. It's heavier to run than the lightweight options, but if you need the full product-analytics stack, it's the only serious open source option.
selectionNotes: We score Privacy Analytics tools on: cookie behavior (none vs fingerprint vs full cookie banner), GDPR/CCPA defaults, page weight (script size affects Core Web Vitals), and real-time capability. For product analytics, we score on the breadth of the feature set, the SDK quality, and the export path so you never get locked in.

intro:
The CRM category is unusually crowded and unusually uneven. Salesforce and HubSpot have trained an entire generation of sales teams to expect a specific UX, and most open source CRMs either ape that UX without the polish (SuiteCRM, EspoCRM, YetiForce) or take a fundamentally different approach (Twenty, Monica, Crater, Krayin).

If you want the closest possible open source analog to Salesforce, SuiteCRM is the answer — it's a fork of the open-sourced SugarCRM Community Edition, has 15+ years of feature development, and runs on a LAMP stack. It's the most full-featured option but also the heaviest. EspoCRM is the lighter, faster alternative with a cleaner UI.

If you want a modern CRM built for how teams actually work today, Twenty is the most exciting new option. It's a rebuild from scratch with a GraphQL API, a Notion-like UI, and a clean data model. Monica is the personal-relationship CRM (think: track your friends, not your sales pipeline). Crater is invoicing-focused if that's your main need.

The honest answer for most small teams: if Salesforce's pricing is killing you, SuiteCRM or EspoCRM will save you thousands. If you don't actually need a CRM and just want to track customers in a spreadsheet-like interface, Baserow or NocoDB will be faster to set up and easier to maintain.
selectionNotes: We score CRM tools on: data model flexibility (can you model your actual sales process?), integration surface (does it have a clean API and webhooks?), reporting capability (can you answer 'what's our MRR by source?'), and the migration path (can you get your data out cleanly?).

intro:
Communication tools are where the open source vs SaaS debate is most personal. Teams that have used Slack for years are skeptical that anything open source can match the polish. Teams that have left Slack because of pricing are skeptical that anything self-hosted can match the UX.

The reality in 2026: the open source options are mostly excellent. The split is between federated/ActivityPub-based platforms (Element/Matrix, Jami) and traditional server-based platforms (Rocket.Chat, Mattermost, Mumble, Jitsi, BigBlueButton, PeerTube). For team chat specifically, Element (Matrix) is the most credible Slack replacement — end-to-end encryption, voice/video, file sharing, and bridges to Slack/Discord/Telegram for cross-org communication.

For voice/video specifically: Jitsi is the de facto open source Zoom alternative (no account needed, share a link, join). BigBlueButton is purpose-built for online learning (whiteboard, breakout rooms, polls). PeerTube is the YouTube alternative — federated via ActivityPub, no ads, no algorithm.

The honest answer for most teams leaving Slack: Element + Jitsi covers chat, voice, video, and screen sharing for most use cases. Self-host both on a single $20/month VPS and you're set. If you need federation with other organizations (so external partners can join without a separate account), Matrix is the only option that does this well.
selectionNotes: We score Communication tools on: message reliability (does it lose messages under load?), search quality (can you actually find old messages?), integration surface (incoming webhooks, bots, REST API), and mobile experience (does the mobile app actually work?).

intro:
Project management is one of the harder categories to get right because teams have wildly different workflows. The open source space here ranges from full Jira replacements (Redmine, Tuleap) to lightweight Kanban boards (Wekan, Kanboard, Focalboard, Taiga) to specialized tools for specific methodologies (OpenProject for traditional PM, Taiga for Scrum/Kanban, Focalboard for personal/notion-like use).

If you're replacing Jira and need issue tracking, Gantt charts, time tracking, and multi-project workflows: Redmine is the most mature, OpenProject is the most modern, Tuleap is the most enterprise. Taiga is the best option for Scrum/Kanban teams who don't need the full PM suite.

For personal use or small teams that just need a Kanban board: Focalboard (from the Mattermost team) has the cleanest Notion-like UX. Wekan is the Trello clone that just works. Kanboard is the minimalist option for power users who want keyboard shortcuts and zero bloat.

For accessibility-focused or ADHD-friendly workflows: Leantime is the only option specifically designed for neurodiverse teams. It minimizes cognitive load and supports how neurodiverse people actually work.

The honest answer: pick Taiga or Focalboard if you're a small team that wants something modern. Pick Redmine or OpenProject if you're replacing Jira and need depth. Don't pick anything heavier than you need.
selectionNotes: We score project management tools on: workflow flexibility (can you model your actual process?), reporting (can you get the metrics your team lead needs?), integration with code repos (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket links, commit references), and the speed of the UI under load (slow tools kill adoption).

intro:
The CMS category is where 'open source' gets complicated. WordPress powers 40%+ of the web and is technically open source, but the ecosystem around it (plugins, themes, hosting) is mostly commercial. Ghost is open source but the managed version is the popular one. The headless CMS space (Strapi, Directus, KeystoneJS, TinaCMS, Decap CMS) is genuinely open source but requires a developer.

For a traditional blog or business site: WordPress is the default. It's been around since 2003, has a theme for everything, and the cost of ownership is the lowest in the industry. Ghost is the modern alternative if you want a faster, cleaner publishing experience (and don't need WordPress's plugin ecosystem). Both are genuinely open source.

For headless / developer-first CMS: Strapi is the most popular Node.js option with a strong admin UI and a flexible data model. Directus wraps any existing SQL database (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, Oracle) with an admin UI and API — unique because it doesn't own your data, it lives in your existing database. KeystoneJS is the developer-favorite for custom Node.js CMS. TinaCMS and Decap CMS are git-based, designed for static sites and Next.js, where content lives in Markdown files in your repo.

For enterprise or compliance-heavy use: Plone (Python) has 20+ years of security track record, accessibility built in (WCAG 2.2 AA), and is used by governments and Fortune 500 companies.

The honest answer: pick WordPress if you want zero developer involvement. Pick Ghost if you want a modern blog. Pick Strapi or Directus if you have developers and want headless. Pick Plone if you need enterprise compliance.
selectionNotes: We score CMS tools on: editor experience (how easy is it for non-technical editors?), content modeling flexibility (can you model your actual content?), API surface (REST/GraphQL quality), and the migration path (can you get your content out as clean Markdown or JSON?).

intro:
Email marketing is one of the categories where open source has the clearest cost advantage. Mailchimp, ConvertKit, and ActiveCampaign all charge $30-100+/month once you have a few thousand subscribers. The open source alternatives charge $0-50/month flat because they use Amazon SES (or similar) for delivery, which costs $0.10 per 1,000 emails.

The split is between full-featured newsletters (Sendy) and self-hosted mail servers (Postal, Stalwart, Mailcow, WildDuck, iRedMail, Mailu). Sendy is the most popular: it's a one-time $69 license, uses Amazon SES for delivery, and has a beautiful UI that matches ConvertKit. The license + SES costs work out to <$10/month for most newsletters.

For self-hosted mail servers (where you actually run the SMTP/IMAP server yourself): Mailcow is the easiest full-stack Docker install, Mailu is the lighter alternative, Stalwart is the modern Rust-based option with JMAP support, Postal is the simplified SendGrid alternative for transactional email.

The honest answer: if you're sending a newsletter and want to escape Mailchimp fees, Sendy + Amazon SES is unbeatable on price (one-time $69 license, $0.10 per 1K emails). If you want full self-hosting of your mail server, Mailcow is the most complete and easiest to deploy.
selectionNotes: We score email marketing tools on: deliverability (will your emails land in inbox, not spam?), subscriber management (segments, tags, suppression lists), automation (drip campaigns, autoresponders), and analytics (open rates, click rates, bounce tracking).

intro:
Auth is one of the categories where the cost savings are most dramatic and the implementation risk is highest. Auth0 charges $240/month for 10K active users. Okta is $2-5/user/month. Both are excellent products — but for a small team or self-hosted stack, those costs add up fast.

The open source alternatives span the full spectrum: full identity providers (Keycloak, Ory, Authentik, Casdoor, Zitadel), lightweight SSO proxies (Authelia), pre-built auth with UI (SuperTokens, Logto), and OAuth2-only libraries (Ory Hydra). Each has different strengths.

For most self-hosted stacks: Keycloak is the most battle-tested option (Red Hat maintains it, thousands of deployments). Authentik is the modern alternative with a cleaner UI. Authelia is the lightweight option for homelabs — single Go binary, sits in front of your apps as a reverse-proxy-level auth.

For SaaS / B2B apps: Ory or Logto. Ory is the CNCF stack (Hydra, Kratos, Keto, Oathkeeper) used by hundreds of SaaS companies. Logto is the newer alternative with a beautiful pre-built sign-in UI that saves weeks of development.

The honest answer: pick Keycloak if you're a homelab or self-hosted shop. Pick Logto or Ory if you're building a SaaS. Pick Authelia if you just want 2FA in front of Grafana and Nextcloud. Don't pick Ory if you're not ready for the operational complexity.
selectionNotes: We score auth tools on: standards compliance (OIDC, OAuth2, SAML, WebAuthn), UI quality (how much custom UI do you need to build?), multi-tenancy support (per-customer identity for B2B), and the migration path (can you get users out cleanly?).

intro:
Search is the category where the technical bar is highest and the right answer depends entirely on your use case. Full-text search at scale (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) is overkill for 95% of applications. SQL FTS is fine for another 4%. The remaining 1% need real search infrastructure.

The split is between general-purpose search servers (Meilisearch, Typesense, OpenSearch, ZincSearch, Manticore, Apache Solr, Vespa), autocomplete-specific engines (Sonic), and log analytics with search (OpenSearch with Dashboards).

For most apps: Meilisearch or Typesense. Both are Rust-based, fast, easy to deploy, and have first-class typo tolerance. Meilisearch has the smoother developer experience; Typesense has the better faceting/filtering story.

For Elasticsearch replacement (after the SSPL license change): OpenSearch is the direct fork maintained by AWS and the Linux Foundation. Same APIs (mostly), same scale, true open source.

For log analytics + search: OpenSearch with OpenSearch Dashboards, or Grafana Loki if you don't need full search.

For autocomplete specifically: Sonic is a single ~30MB Rust binary purpose-built for typeahead search, used in production by Opera for browser search.

The honest answer: pick Meilisearch or Typesense for app search. Pick OpenSearch for log analytics. Don't pick Elasticsearch unless you have a specific reason — the licensing risk is real.
selectionNotes: We score search engines on: indexing speed (how fast can you reindex?), query latency at scale, typo tolerance quality, faceting/filtering capability, and operational complexity (single binary vs distributed cluster).

intro:
Storage is where open source genuinely wins. Nextcloud, Seafile, MinIO, Syncthing, OwnCloud, FileRun, Pydio, Garage — there's a serious open source answer for almost every storage use case, and they're often cheaper and more flexible than the SaaS alternatives.

The split is between file sync & share (Nextcloud, Seafile, OwnCloud, FileRun, Pydio), peer-to-peer sync (Syncthing), and object storage (MinIO, Garage). Each has different strengths.

For Dropbox/Drive replacement: Nextcloud is the most full-featured (file sync, calendar, contacts, office docs via Collabora/OnlyOffice, mobile apps). Seafile is the faster alternative for large libraries. OwnCloud is the more enterprise-focused option with federation and E2E encryption. FileRun has the cleanest Google Drive-like UI.

For peer-to-peer file sync (no server, no cloud): Syncthing is the answer. It's the de facto standard, used by tens of thousands of people, and works across all platforms. The trade-off is no central admin — it's just direct device-to-device sync.

For S3-compatible object storage (S3 replacement): MinIO is the de facto answer, scales from single server to distributed clusters, 100% S3 API compatible. Garage is the lighter Rust-based alternative designed for small clusters (3-10 nodes).

The honest answer: Nextcloud if you want the full Google Workspace alternative. Seafile if you only need file sync and want it faster than Nextcloud. Syncthing if you don't want a server at all. MinIO if you want S3 without paying AWS.
selectionNotes: We score storage tools on: sync speed and reliability (do large files sync without corruption?), mobile app quality (does the iOS/Android app actually work?), collaboration features (sharing, comments, simultaneous editing), and the backup/restore story (can you get your data out cleanly?).

intro:
Workflow automation is dominated by Zapier and Make, both of which charge per task ($10-100+/month for any meaningful volume). The open source alternatives are full-featured and free, but require you to host them.

The split is between visual no-code automation (n8n, Activepieces), developer-first platforms (Windmill), and serious workflow orchestrators (Apache Airflow, Temporal, Kestra, Argo Workflows, Apache Hop). These serve very different use cases.

For Zapier/Make replacement: n8n is the most popular, with 400+ integrations and a fair-code license. Activepieces is the newer open source alternative with cleaner TypeScript pieces.

For developer platforms: Windmill turns scripts (Python, TypeScript, Go, Bash) into workflows, schedules, API endpoints, and UIs — the developer-first answer to Airflow. Temporal handles long-running workflows and durable execution (the standard for microservice orchestration).

For data pipelines: Apache Airflow is the original and most widely adopted. Kestra is the modern declarative alternative with better UX. Argo Workflows is the Kubernetes-native answer if your stack is K8s.

The honest answer: pick n8n if you're replacing Zapier. Pick Windmill if you're a developer who wants to write scripts not click buttons. Pick Airflow if you need a battle-tested data orchestrator. Pick Temporal if you need microservice orchestration.
selectionNotes: We score automation tools on: integration count and quality, visual editor UX (how easy is it for non-developers?), error handling (what happens when a step fails?), and the scheduler reliability (does it run jobs at the right time?).

intro:
Monitoring is one of the categories where the open source vs SaaS choice has the biggest operational impact. Datadog, New Relic, and Splunk all charge per host per month, which adds up fast for any meaningful infrastructure. The open source alternatives are mature and self-hostable.

The split is between uptime monitoring (Uptime Kuma), full observability platforms (SigNoz, Netdata), and the heavyweight systems (Prometheus + Grafana + Loki stack, which we don't list here because they're well-known).

For uptime monitoring (replacing Uptime Robot or Pingdom): Uptime Kuma is the answer. Beautiful Vue 3 UI, 100+ notification types (Slack, Discord, Telegram, email, webhook), HTTP/TCP/ping/DNS/push/Docker/database checks, status pages. Self-host on a $5 VPS.

For application observability (replacing Datadog or New Relic): SigNoz is the open source answer. Logs, metrics, and traces in one place, OpenTelemetry-native, ClickHouse-backed for fast queries. Netdata is the real-time infrastructure monitoring option (per-second metrics, beautiful dashboards, zero configuration).

The honest answer: Uptime Kuma for uptime checks, SigNoz for application observability, Netdata for real-time server monitoring. All three together cover 90% of what Datadog does, for free, self-hosted.
selectionNotes: We score monitoring tools on: query performance at scale (can it handle your metric volume?), alerting flexibility (can you route alerts to the right channel?), UI responsiveness (does the dashboard stay snappy?), and the OpenTelemetry support (the modern standard for traces and metrics).

intro:
Code hosting is the category where 'self-hosted GitHub' has finally become realistic. Gitea and Forgejo are both fast, lightweight, GitHub-like, and can run on a Raspberry Pi. The old alternatives (GitLab CE) are still available but heavy.

For self-hosted GitHub replacement: Gitea (now run by a for-profit company) and Forgejo (community-governed soft fork). Both have issues, pull requests, packages, actions (CI/CD), wikis, releases. The choice between them is mostly governance: Gitea has more polish and faster releases, Forgejo has stronger community governance and a clearer open source commitment.

For teams currently on github.com: the migration is well-supported. Gitea has an import tool that pulls in repos, issues, labels, milestones, comments, releases, and wiki pages from GitHub.

The honest answer: pick Forgejo if open source governance matters to you (this is what Codeberg and many open source projects migrated to). Pick Gitea if you want the slightly more polished UI and faster release cadence. Don't pick GitLab CE unless you need its full DevOps platform — it's overkill for just code hosting.
selectionNotes: We score code hosting tools on: speed of the UI (Gitea/Forgejo are both fast, GitLab is slower), resource footprint (Gitea/Forgejo run on 1GB RAM, GitLab needs 4GB+), action runner support (CI/CD), and the import/migration path (can you move from GitHub?).

intro:
Business intelligence is dominated by Tableau, Looker, Power BI, and Mode. All are excellent products. All are expensive at scale. The open source alternatives have matured significantly in the last 5 years.

The split is between SQL-first BI tools (Metabase, Apache Superset, Redash), dbt-native BI (Lightdash), and chart libraries you build into your own app (not in scope here).

For most teams replacing Tableau/Looker/Power BI: Metabase is the answer. It's the easiest to deploy, has the cleanest UX for non-technical users, supports 20+ data sources out of the box, and has a generous free cloud tier. Self-host on a small VM.

Apache Superset is the enterprise alternative originally built at Airbnb. More powerful SQL IDE, 40+ chart types, 30+ data sources, but more complex to deploy and harder for non-technical users.

For dbt-based data teams: Lightdash is purpose-built. You define metrics in your dbt project (YAML), Lightdash turns them into dashboards. This is the modern approach: metrics-as-code, version-controlled, integrated with your data transformation workflow.

The honest answer: pick Metabase if you need BI for a non-technical team and want it working in an afternoon. Pick Apache Superset if you need enterprise features and have data analysts who can handle a steeper learning curve. Pick Lightdash if you use dbt and want metrics as code.
selectionNotes: We score BI tools on: SQL editor quality (power users need a real IDE), visualization variety (how many chart types?), dashboard UX (can non-technical users actually use it?), and the embedding API (can you embed dashboards in your own product?).
